result.summary: Achilles learns of Patroclus's death and is overcome with grief; Thetis comes from the sea and promises new armour. Achilles shows himself at the trench and terrifies the Trojans, Hector rejects Polydamas's advice to retreat, and Thetis gets Vulcan to forge the armour, including the great shield.

scenes.title: Antilochus brings the news
scenes.summary: Antilochus tells Achilles that Patroclus is dead and Hector holds his armour. Achilles pours dust on his head and lies groaning.
scenes.stakes: Achilles faces the loss of his closest friend and risks despair, even suicide.

scenes.title: Thetis comforts Achilles
scenes.summary: Thetis and the Nereids rise from the sea. Achilles vows to kill Hector, and Thetis warns him his own death will follow, but promises armour from Vulcan.
scenes.stakes: Achilles will die soon after Hector; Thetis will lose her son.

scenes.title: Achilles shouts at the trench
scenes.summary: Hector nearly drags off the body until Iris, sent by Juno, tells Achilles to show himself. Minerva crowns him with fire, his shout routs the Trojans, and the body is recovered.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus's body risks mutilation by Hector and the Trojans.

place.name: the trench before the Achaean wall

scenes.title: Trojan assembly: Polydamas and Hector
scenes.summary: Polydamas urges retreat into Troy. Hector refuses, and the Trojans, robbed of wit by Minerva, applaud him.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk destruction by Achilles on the open plain.

place.name: the Trojan camp on the plain

scenes.title: Mourning Patroclus
scenes.summary: Achilles vows to behead twelve Trojans and not bury Patroclus until Hector is dead. The body is washed and laid out, while Jove and Juno bicker.
scenes.stakes: Achilles has promised vengeance and acknowledges his own death far from home.

scenes.title: Thetis at Vulcan's house
scenes.summary: Charis welcomes Thetis. Vulcan recalls how Thetis and Eurynome saved him after his fall and agrees to help.
scenes.stakes: Thetis needs help for her doomed son.

scenes.title: Thetis's plea; the forge
scenes.summary: Thetis recounts her sorrows and begs armour for Achilles. Vulcan promises it and begins work at his bellows.
scenes.stakes: Achilles has no armour and a near end.

scenes.title: The shield of Achilles
scenes.summary: Vulcan forges the shield with the heavens, two cities, farming scenes, herds and a dance, then breastplate, helmet and greaves. Thetis carries them off.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles condemns anger, sweeter than honey yet destructive.
Hector's fatalistic view that the slayer may be slain.
Opens the famous description of the shield's cosmos.

analysis.text: Achilles turns from wrath at Agamemnon to wrath at Hector, accepting early death for vengeance and glory.
The shield's scenes of marriage, law courts, farming and war give a picture of a Greek world at peace and at war, and is a famous example of ekphrasis.

legacy.text: The shield of Achilles is the model of ekphrasis; W. H. Auden's poem 'The Shield of Achilles' (1952) reworks it.
The film Troy (2004) includes Achilles's grief over a slain companion, though it changes the story.

fun_facts.text: Vulcan's golden handmaids who think and speak are an early literary vision of artificial beings.

language_notes.text: "As it were a flaming fire" compares the battle's intensity to a blaze; it continues the fighting from the end of Book 17.
Thetis had earlier told Achilles that the best of the Myrmidons would die while he still lived. Achilles now fears this has come true.
Achilles had told Patroclus to drive the Trojans from the ships, then return, and not fight Hector. Patroclus ignored this warning.
"Refuse" here means the dirt or ashes; "comely" means handsome.
"Plunge a knife into his own throat" means Antilochus fears Achilles will commit suicide from grief.
"The old man her father" is Nereus, the sea-god, who lives in the depths and is father of the fifty Nereids.
Refers to Achilles' earlier prayer to Jove, in Book 1, that the Achaeans suffer in his absence to honour him after Agamemnon's insult.
"What boots it to me" means "what good is it to me"; "vouchsafed" means graciously granted.
The armour was a wedding gift to Peleus from the gods; Patroclus wore it into battle and Hector took it from his body.
"Bootless" means useless or without profit.
Hercules, Jove's son, was hounded by Juno's anger throughout his life and died despite Jove's love.
"Vaunt" means boast; "the press of battle" is the thick crowd of fighting.
Mars's servant: Patroclus is called a servant (Greek therapon, attendant) of Mars, the war god, meaning a devoted warrior. Mars is the Greek Ares.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans. Ilius is Troy.
Refers to Thetis's promise to bring new armour made by Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), since Hector took Achilles' armour from Patroclus.
'Which in battle may hardly be' means such respite is rare in war.
Aegis: a fearsome divine shield or cloak, tasselled and associated with Jove and Minerva, that terrifies enemies.
Oceanus is the river believed to encircle the world; the sun was imagined to set into it.
"Look both before and after" means he could weigh past and future, seeing consequences. It is a Homeric formula for prudence.
"Bide" means to stay or wait; "this man" refers to Achilles, who had withdrawn from the fighting over his quarrel with Agamemnon.
"Sallies forth" means makes a sudden sortie; "we shall have knowledge of him in good earnest" means we will learn what he is truly like, to our cost.
"Meat for dogs and vultures" refers to unburied corpses, a dreaded fate in Homeric warfare. "May I never live to hear it" is a wish to be spared the news.
"Whithers" is archaic for "in every direction"; the phrase describes Achilles driving his chariot horses back and forth below the walls.
Phrygia and Meonia (Lydia) were regions of Asia Minor. Trojan wealth was being sold there to pay for the long war.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted; "prate" means to chatter foolishly; "in this fool's wise" means in this foolish manner.
Mars, the god of war, is impartial: he deals out death evenly, so even a victor can be killed.
"Dingle and dell" both mean small wooded valleys; the paired words stress how thoroughly the lion searches.
Menoetius was Patroclus' father; Opoeis was his home city in Locris. Achilles had promised to bring Patroclus home safely.
A bier is a stand or frame on which a corpse is laid before burial.
"Dardanus" refers to the Trojan people, named for their ancestor Dardanus; the women are captives taken from nearby cities.
A tripod here is a three-legged cauldron for heating water over a fire.
"Sister-wife" reflects that Juno is both Jove's sister and his wife; in Greek myth she was the daughter of Saturn like him.
"Star-bespangled" means studded with stars; the house is described as shining like the heavens. "Imperishable" means it never decays.
A tripod is a three-legged cauldron or stand, a common prestige item and prize in Homeric society.
Charis (Grace) is Vulcan's wife here. "Of graceful head-dress" is a fixed descriptive phrase for her.
Refers to Vulcan being thrown from heaven as a newborn because he was lame. His mother is Juno, though she is not named here.
"Spiral armlets" are coiled bracelets worn on the arm, typical of the ornaments Vulcan crafts.
"Requital" means repayment, here a return of a favor.
"Lustily" means vigorously. "Plying" means working busily.
Thetis was forced by the gods to marry the mortal Peleus; the son of Saturn is Jove (Zeus), who arranged this.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted; Thetis says the gods gave her a son, though the gift brought her grief.
Ilius is Ilium, i.e. Troy; "the Trojans" are its defenders.
Refers to the embassy of Book 9, when Achaean elders offered Achilles gifts to rejoin the war and he refused.
The son of Menoetius is Patroclus, killed with Apollo's help; Hector then stripped Achilles' armour from his body.
"Haply" means perhaps; "greaves" are shin guards, here fastened with ankle-clasps.
A baldric is a belt or strap worn over the shoulder, here the shield's carrying strap.
The Pleiads, Hyads and Orion are star groups; the Bear (the Wain, or wagon) never sets below the horizon, so it never 'dips' into Oceanus.
Hymen is the wedding cry or song, also the name of the god of marriage.
Blood-money is compensation paid to a victim's family for a killing, so as to avoid a blood feud.
A talent was a weight of gold, a large sum; here it is the prize for the fairest judgement.
Fate here translates a personified doom (Ker) who drags off the dying; 'bedrabbled' means soaked and soiled.
The Linos-song was a mournful folk song for Linos, a youth who died young, often sung at vintage.
Daedalus was the legendary Cretan craftsman; Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos of Cnossus. The 'green' is a dancing floor.
The 'famed lame god' is Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), the smith god, who is lame; Achilles' mother is Thetis.

context_notes.text: Antilochus is Nestor's son and a fast runner, so he is a fitting messenger.
Myrmidons were Achilles' followers from Phthia. Thetis is his divine mother, a sea goddess.
Pouring dust on the head was a customary sign of extreme mourning in Homeric Greece.
The Nereids are sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus; the catalogue of names is a traditional epic device.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' followers from Phthia, whose ships lie drawn up on the beach.
Thetis knows a prophecy that Achilles will die soon after Hector does.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the smith-god who makes the gods' finest metalwork.
Juno (the Greek Hera) favours the Greeks and acts behind Jove's back, since he had forbidden gods to interfere.
Cutting off a head and displaying it on stakes was a feared outrage, denying the dead proper burial.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is called grey-eyed, a standard description of her.
Polydamas and Hector were born on the same night, a bond that explains his frankness. He often gives Hector sound advice that Hector rejects.
Saturn is the father of Jove (Greek Zeus). Hector takes Jove's favour as proof that the Trojans should keep fighting by the ships.
Pallas Minerva (Greek Athena) sided with the Greeks and here clouds the Trojans' judgement, sealing their doom.
Achilles knows from his mother Thetis that he is fated to die at Troy soon after Hector.
Human sacrifice of captives at a hero's funeral is shocking even in the poem; it shows the extent of Achilles' rage.
Washing and anointing the dead with oil was the normal preparation of a body before burial.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the divine smith, lame from birth, who builds the gods' palaces and weapons. He will now make new armour for Achilles.
Oceanus is the great river encircling the world. Eurynome is a sea goddess, daughter of Oceanus, who sheltered Vulcan with Thetis.
Vulcan's golden handmaids are early artificial beings, mechanical helpers that think and speak, as in his self-moving tripods.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the divine smith. Thetis came to his house, where she had been kindly received in the past.
Vulcan's bellows work on their own at his will, one of several self-moving devices in his workshop.
Elders judged disputes in the public assembly; the staves were held by whoever spoke, marking the right to give judgement.
Mars is the god of war and Pallas Minerva the goddess of wise battle; here they lead the city's ambushers.
Oceanus was imagined as a great river encircling the world, so it fittingly rings the shield's edge.

literary_notes.text: The reader knows Achilles' foreboding is true and that the messenger has arrived, while Achilles still only suspects.
Grief is described as a dark cloud falling on Achilles, suggesting it overwhelms him and blots out everything else.
"All huge and hugely" stresses Achilles' enormous body and the scale of his collapse.
Thetis likens Achilles to a sapling and a garden plant, stressing her tender nurture and the loss of his promise.
Thetis's words link Hector's death to Achilles' own, anticipating his fate beyond the poem's end.
Anger is compared to smoke rising in the soul, and its sweetness to honey, showing how seductive and hollow rage is.
"Silver-footed" is Thetis's fixed Homeric epithet, lending her dignity as she agrees to help.
Hector's advance is compared to a furnace flame, stressing its destructive, unstoppable heat.
The Ajaxes are likened to shepherds unable to drive off a hungry lion, showing Hector's ferocity and the body as prey.
The beacon fires of a besieged island city mirror the blaze on Achilles' head, signalling desperate need for help.
Achilles' voice is like a trumpet at a city's alarm, making his cry a sound of doom.
Achilles' failure to welcome Patroclus home hints at the grief and vengeance that follow.
Polydamas shows his caution and foresight by naming Achilles as the real danger and predicting an assault on the city.
Hector's scornful question dismisses Polydamas' caution and shows his pride and impatience for glory.
The narrator reveals divine interference the Trojans cannot see, so the reader knows their applause leads to disaster.
The rejection of wise counsel hints at the Trojans' coming defeat and Hector's death.
Achilles' grief and rage are compared to a lion robbed of its cubs, making his sorrow fierce and dangerous.
Achilles speaks directly to the dead Patroclus, as if he could hear the vow.
Jove sarcastically accuses Juno of caring for the Achaeans like kin, mocking her motives in stirring Achilles.
Juno defends herself proudly, stressing her rank and her anger at Troy, which shows her stubborn, vengeful nature.
Self-moving golden-wheeled tripods vividly show Vulcan's marvelous craft and the wonder of divine technology.
"Silver-footed" is Thetis's fixed epithet, linking her to the sea's shimmer and her divine beauty.
Vulcan speaks of his rejection bitterly yet gratefully, showing a humble character that remembers kindness.
Calling the lame, hobbling craftsman a "mighty monster" while stressing his thin legs contrasts his power and skill with his bodily weakness.
Vulcan repeats his wife's welcome almost word for word, a formulaic Homeric echo showing the ritual courtesy of hospitality.
Thetis opens with a question that stresses her suffering as unmatched and wins sympathy.
Achilles is likened to a sapling, and in the next sentence to a tended plant, suggesting rapid growth and a mother's care.
Vulcan wishes he could hide Achilles from death as surely as he can supply armour, admitting the limit of divine power and hinting that fate cannot be avoided.
The bellows are bidden to "do their office" and respond to Vulcan's will like obedient servants.
The two cities, one at peace and one at war, set up a contrast that runs through the shield.
The golden field looks freshly ploughed, praising the smith's art as nearly beyond nature.
The herdsmen, meant to guard the cattle, are helpless, while the dogs hold back, showing fear overcoming duty.
The dancers' circling is compared to a potter testing his wheel, a homely image of smooth motion.
Thetis darting like a falcon conveys her speed and eagerness to carry the armour to her son.
